title: From a single neuron to the GPUs and LLMs behind modern AI
tagline: An interactive course that takes complete beginners from the silicon up to how modern large language models work.
audience: Complete beginners who want to reach an advanced level of understanding. No math background needed.

format.summary: Every module is a short, hands-on lesson. The explanation is in the middle of the page, an interactive simulation is on the right, and every course and module is always visible in the left sidebar.
eachModuleContains: A plain-language introduction with hover-to-explain glossary terms
An interactive simulation with a task to complete
A short quiz with explanations (the module counts as done when all answers are correct)
An optional 'Go deeper' section with technical detail and real hardware numbers
format.progress: Saved in the browser. Each course shows how many modules are done.

courses.title: How Do Machines Learn?
courses.description: Start here: what AI really is, how machines learn patterns from data, what a neuron does, how a network learns from its mistakes, and the difference between training a model and using it.

modules.title: What is AI? How it differs from traditional software
modules.goal: Understand the big difference between AI and normal software: AI learns its rules from examples.
modules.summary: Traditional software follows rules a person wrote. AI is shown examples with the right answers and works out the rules itself, which wins on fuzzy problems like spam, faces and language.

simulation.name: Spam sorter: rules vs learning
simulation.description: Six new emails to sort. On one side you switch on hand-written rules ('contains free', 'has !!!'); on the other a model learns a score per word from up to 12 labelled examples. A table shows each email's verdict from both approaches.
whatYouDo: Switch hand-written spam rules on and off
Slide how many labelled examples the model learns from
simulation.task: Try the rules, then let the model learn from all 12 examples: the rules get at most 4 of 6 right, the learned model all 6.

keyTakeaways: Traditional software follows rules a person wrote; AI learns its own rules from examples.
A learned model is only as good as its examples, and it can make mistakes.

modules.title: Machine learning, deep learning and LLMs
modules.goal: Know what AI, machine learning, deep learning and LLMs mean, and how they fit inside each other.
modules.summary: The terms nest like boxes: AI contains machine learning (learning from examples), which contains deep learning (many-layered neural networks), which contains LLMs (deep networks trained on text).

simulation.name: Sort the AI family
simulation.description: Seven real systems (a calculator, a chess rule engine, a spam filter, face unlock, a chatbot…) to sort into Not AI, AI without learning, machine learning, deep learning or LLM. Correct answers appear as numbered dots inside nested circles, with a short explanation.
whatYouDo: Pick the smallest circle each system belongs to
Read why each answer is right
simulation.task: Sort all 7 systems correctly.

keyTakeaways: Every LLM is deep learning, all deep learning is machine learning, and all machine learning is AI.
'Deep' means a neural network with many layers.

modules.title: Data, patterns and predictions
modules.goal: See how a model finds a pattern in data and uses it to make predictions, and why more examples help.
modules.summary: A model finds a pattern in examples (house size vs price) and applies it to new cases. With too few examples the pattern is wrong; with many, random quirks cancel out.

simulation.name: House price pattern
simulation.description: A chart of house sales with the best straight line through them. Five new houses show how far each prediction misses, and a slider predicts the price of any size.
whatYouDo: Learn the pattern from 2, 5 or 20 examples
Predict prices for new house sizes
simulation.task: Compare 2 and 20 examples: the average miss drops from about €29k to about €8k.

keyTakeaways: A prediction is the learned pattern applied to a new case.
Judge a model on new cases, not on the examples it learned from.

modules.title: Meet the neuron: inputs, weights and bias
modules.goal: See that a neuron just multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up and adds a bias.
modules.summary: A neuron multiplies each input by a weight (how much it matters), adds them up and adds a bias. Its weights and bias are its parameters: everything it knows.

simulation.name: Beach-day neuron
simulation.description: A neuron with three inputs (sunshine, friends coming, homework left) decides whether to go to the beach. Line thickness and colour show the weights; the full calculation is shown for Saturday and Tuesday.
whatYouDo: Set three weights and the bias with sliders
Switch between Saturday and Tuesday
simulation.task: Make the neuron say 'go' on Saturday and 'stay home' on Tuesday.

keyTakeaways: Output = inputs × weights, added up, plus the bias.
Weights and biases are the only things a network learns.

modules.title: How networks learn: loss and gradient descent
modules.goal: Understand how a network finds good weights by itself: measure the mistakes, then nudge the weights downhill.
modules.summary: The loss measures how wrong the model is. The gradient points downhill, and gradient descent takes small steps that way until the loss is low. The step size must be just right.

simulation.name: Rolling down the loss valley
simulation.description: A one-weight model converts kilometres to miles. The loss curve is drawn as a valley with a ball for the current weight and a trail of past steps.
whatYouDo: Choose tiny, good or too-big steps
Take one step or ten at a time
simulation.task: Get the loss below 0.01, then see too-big steps overshoot and blow up.

keyTakeaways: Gradient descent: small step downhill, measure again, repeat.
Too small is slow; too big overshoots and the mistakes explode.

modules.title: Hidden layers and deep neural networks
modules.goal: See why networks need hidden layers, and how stacking layers makes them deep.
modules.summary: A single neuron can only draw one straight line. Hidden neurons each draw a line and the next layer combines them into curved shapes. Stacking layers makes a network deep.

simulation.name: Circle sorter
simulation.description: 140 dots, inside or outside a circle, sorted by three networks. The map shades what each network calls 'inside' and draws every neuron's line, next to a network diagram, the accuracy and the parameter count, with real networks for comparison.
whatYouDo: Switch between no hidden layer, 3 and 8 hidden neurons
simulation.task: Reach 95% or more: no hidden layer gets 61%, 3 neurons 89%, 8 neurons 99%.

keyTakeaways: Hidden neurons combine straight lines into curved shapes.
More neurons and layers mean many more parameters.

modules.title: Training vs inference
modules.goal: Know the two jobs of every model, training and inference, and why both need huge amounts of math.
modules.summary: Training runs a forward pass, compares and runs a backward pass to change the weights, over huge amounts of data. Inference only runs the forward pass with frozen weights. Both lead straight into Track 2: why AI needs GPUs.

simulation.name: Train it, then use it
simulation.description: Training mode trains the km-to-miles model one example at a time, showing the forward pass, the comparison and the backward pass. Inference mode asks the frozen model questions. A model picker shows the operations and memory for a 1-weight model, a handwriting reader and Llama 3 8B.
whatYouDo: Train on examples and watch the weight change
Ask the frozen model questions
Compare the cost for real models
simulation.task: Train at least 3 times, ask the model once, then pick Llama 3 8B (16 billion operations per answer).

keyTakeaways: Training changes the weights; inference only reads them.
Every weight must be stored and used for every answer: the reason AI needs special hardware.

courses.title: Why Does AI Run on GPUs?
courses.description: Why a graphics chip became the engine of AI: parallel workers, matrix multiplication, memory bottlenecks, number precision and how much hardware big models need.

modules.title: AI is mostly multiplication
modules.goal: See why AI needs an enormous amount of very simple math.
modules.summary: A neuron only multiplies and adds. A big model repeats this billions of times: producing one word costs about 2 operations per parameter.

simulation.name: Operations counter
simulation.description: Pick a network, from the 4-parameter beach neuron of Track 1 up to GPT-3 (175 billion weights). The simulation counts the multiplications and additions needed for one word and shows how long that takes for a person with a calculator, a desktop CPU and an AI GPU (NVIDIA H100), on a logarithmic bar chart.
whatYouDo: Choose bigger and bigger models
Compare the time per word for a human, a CPU and a GPU
simulation.task: Finish with GPT-3: one word needs about 350 billion operations, over 11,000 years by hand.

keyTakeaways: Neural networks do almost nothing except multiply and add, but a staggering number of times.
Producing one word costs about 2 operations per parameter.
Training costs vastly more than answering.
The winning chip is the one that does the most simple operations at once.

modules.title: CPU vs GPU: experts vs an army
modules.goal: Understand the different design ideas behind a CPU and a GPU, and when each one wins.
modules.summary: A CPU is a few brilliant, fast cores; a GPU is thousands of simple ones working in parallel. Neural networks are lots of identical, independent jobs, which is exactly what GPUs are built for.

simulation.name: CPU vs GPU race
simulation.description: An animated race between a CPU (8 fast workers) and a GPU (512 slower workers with a start-up cost). Each job is a cell in a grid that fills up as work completes.
whatYouDo: Choose the number of jobs (16 to 4,096)
Choose independent jobs or jobs that each depend on the previous result
Start the race and read the verdict
simulation.task: Find a setting where the CPU wins and one where the GPU wins.

keyTakeaways: CPU: few, fast, flexible cores. GPU: thousands of simple cores.
A GPU has a start-up cost, so tiny jobs are not worth sending to it.
If every step depends on the previous one, extra workers cannot help.

modules.title: Neural networks are matrix multiplication
modules.goal: See that a whole layer of neurons is one matrix multiplication, which is exactly what GPUs are best at.
modules.summary: Put a layer's weights in a grid and computing every neuron becomes one matrix multiplication. Every output is independent, and batching many inputs turns it into a large grid-times-grid operation.

simulation.name: Layer as a matrix
simulation.description: A small network (3 inputs, 4 neurons) drawn next to its weight matrix, input matrix and output matrix. Selecting a neuron highlights the matching row, column and result, and shows the calculation.
whatYouDo: Click each neuron or output cell
Switch from one input to a batch of 4 inputs
simulation.task: Explore all four neurons to see that every output is one row times one column.

keyTakeaways: A layer of neurons = weight matrix × input vector; with a batch it becomes matrix × matrix.
Every output number is independent: perfect for parallel workers.

modules.title: Memory is the real bottleneck
modules.goal: Discover that a GPU is often waiting for data, not doing math.
modules.summary: A GPU can compute far faster than its memory can feed it. Arithmetic intensity (operations per byte loaded) decides whether the math units are busy or idle.

simulation.name: Roofline explorer
simulation.description: A roofline chart with real NVIDIA H100 numbers (about 989 trillion operations per second, 3.35 TB/s memory). A dot shows where a workload lands, with a gauge of how busy the GPU's math units are.
whatYouDo: Pick real workloads: adding two lists, a chatbot for 1 user, for 64 users, a large training multiply
Slide the operations-per-byte value
simulation.task: Find a workload where the GPU is less than 1% busy and one where it reaches 100%.

keyTakeaways: Low arithmetic intensity means waiting for memory.
A chatbot answering one user is memory-bound; batching many users fills the GPU.

modules.title: The memory hierarchy
modules.goal: Learn the layers of memory in a GPU, and why 'close and small' beats 'far and big'.
modules.summary: From registers to shared memory, L2 cache, HBM, CPU memory and SSD: each step down is bigger but much slower. The model has to live in HBM.

simulation.name: Memory ladder
simulation.description: A ladder of six memory levels with sizes and speeds, plus a kitchen analogy: if reading a register took 1 second, HBM would take minutes and an SSD days. Fetching from a level animates a data packet travelling for a proportional time.
whatYouDo: Fetch data from different levels and compare the waiting times
simulation.task: Fetch from the registers, from GPU memory (HBM) and from the SSD.

keyTakeaways: Faster memory is smaller and closer to the workers.
If a model doesn't fit in GPU memory, it becomes dramatically slower.

modules.title: Threads, warps and SMs
modules.goal: Understand how work is organised on a GPU: threads, warps, blocks and SMs.
modules.summary: Thousands of threads run the same program. Threads move in lockstep teams of 32 (warps), and blocks of work are spread over the GPU's streaming multiprocessors (SMs).

simulation.name: Scheduler and warp divergence
simulation.description: Part 1 spreads blocks of work over 4 SMs in rounds and shows how busy the SMs are, revealing the 'tail effect'. Part 2 shows a 32-thread warp meeting an 'if': when threads disagree, the warp runs both paths one after the other.
whatYouDo: Change the number of blocks
Change how many threads take the 'if' branch
simulation.task: Choose 8 or more blocks that keep every SM busy in every round.

keyTakeaways: Work that doesn't split evenly leaves SMs idle in the last round.
Different branches inside a warp cost extra passes; neural network math has almost none.

modules.title: Tiling: reuse data before you drop it
modules.goal: Learn the most important trick in GPU programming: load a piece of data once, then reuse it many times.
modules.summary: Copying small tiles of each matrix into fast memory and reusing them cuts the trips to slow memory, as long as the tiles still fit.

simulation.name: Tiled matrix multiplication
simulation.description: An animated 8×8 matrix multiplication. Highlighted tiles of A and B are copied into fast memory while a tile of C is built up. Counters show the trips to slow memory and how full the fast memory is.
whatYouDo: Pick a tile size (1×1, 2×2, 4×4, 8×8)
Run the multiplication and compare the memory trips
simulation.task: Run the biggest tile that still fits: 4×4 needs 256 trips instead of 1,024.

keyTakeaways: The same result can cost very different amounts of memory traffic.
Fast AI libraries such as cuBLAS and FlashAttention are largely clever tiling.

modules.title: Number precision and tensor cores
modules.goal: See how storing numbers with fewer bits saves memory and gains speed, and what it costs.
modules.summary: FP32, BF16, FP16, FP8, INT8 and INT4 trade range and precision for memory and speed. Fewer bits mean faster tensor-core math and smaller models.

simulation.name: Number format comparison
simulation.description: Type any number and see how six formats store it: the bit layout (sign, exponent, mantissa), the stored value, the rounding error, the memory a 7-billion-weight model would need and the H100 speed for that format.
whatYouDo: Type numbers or pick presets
Watch overflow and rounding errors appear
simulation.task: Find a number FP16 can't store (above 65,504) but BF16 can.

keyTakeaways: Exponent bits = range; mantissa bits = precision.
BF16 keeps FP32's range with fewer digits, which is why it is popular for training.

modules.title: How many GPUs does a model need?
modules.goal: Put it all together: estimate the memory, the number of GPUs and the speed for real models.
modules.summary: Memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter (plus extra), single-user speed ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ model size, and training needs about 16 bytes per parameter.

simulation.name: GPU sizing calculator
simulation.description: Choose running or training, a model size (1B to 405B), a number format and a GPU (RTX 4090 to B200). The calculator shows the memory needed, the number of GPUs (drawn as a rack) and the top speed in tokens per second.
whatYouDo: Combine model size, number format and GPU
Switch between running and training
simulation.task: Make a 70B model run on a single GPU (it fits in 80 GB with 4-bit weights).

keyTakeaways: Quantization lets big models fit on fewer GPUs and run faster.
Training needs roughly 8× more memory than running in BF16, before counting activations.

courses.title: How Does ChatGPT Actually Work?
courses.description: How a chatbot turns your words into an answer: tokens, embeddings, attention, the transformer, sampling, training, the KV cache and quantization.

modules.title: Predicting the next word
modules.goal: Understand the one simple job every LLM does: guess the next word.
modules.summary: An LLM gives every possible next word a probability, picks one, adds it and repeats. Every answer comes from this loop.

simulation.name: Tiny next-word model
simulation.description: A miniature language model learned from 12 sentences. It shows the probability of each possible next word as bars; you build a sentence by clicking words or letting the model pick at random.
whatYouDo: Click the next word yourself or let the model choose
Look at the sentences it learned from
simulation.task: Build a sentence of at least 6 words ending with a full stop.

keyTakeaways: An LLM predicts the next piece of text again and again.
Its knowledge comes from patterns in its training text.

modules.title: Tokenization: text to numbers
modules.goal: See how text becomes the numbers a model can work with, and why words get cut into pieces.
modules.summary: A tokenizer cuts text into tokens with ID numbers. Byte-pair encoding learns its vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of symbols.

simulation.name: Byte-pair encoding trainer
simulation.description: A real byte-pair-encoding tokenizer trained in the browser on a small word list. Your text is shown as coloured tokens with their IDs, next to letter and token counts and the list of merges learned so far.
whatYouDo: Slide the number of merges from 0 to 40
Type your own text, including unseen words
simulation.task: Use at least 20 merges and reach 3 or more letters per token.

keyTakeaways: Common words become one token; rare words are split into pieces.
In English one token is about 4 characters, roughly ¾ of a word.

modules.title: Embeddings: meaning as a map
modules.goal: See how a model turns each token into a point on a 'map of meaning'.
modules.summary: Each token becomes a list of numbers (a vector). Similar meanings sit close together, and directions on the map carry meaning.

simulation.name: Map of meaning
simulation.description: A 2-D map of words in three groups (people, animals, food). Word math draws arrows on the map and finds the nearest word; clicking a word lists its nearest neighbours.
whatYouDo: Build word equations such as puppy − dog + cat
Click words to see their neighbours
simulation.task: Compute king − man + woman (it lands on queen).

keyTakeaways: An embedding is a list of numbers that stands for a token's meaning.
Embeddings are learned during training, not hand-labelled.

modules.title: Attention: which words matter
modules.goal: Understand attention: how each word gathers information from the words that matter for it.
modules.summary: Each word scores how relevant every other word is; softmax turns the scores into percentages, and the word mixes in information in those proportions.

simulation.name: Attention explorer
simulation.description: The sentence 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired / wide'. Clicking a word shades the others by how much attention they receive, with a table of relevance scores and softmax percentages.
whatYouDo: Click any word to make it the query
Switch the ending between 'tired' and 'wide'
simulation.task: Click 'it' in both versions: it attends to 'animal' with 'tired' and to 'street' with 'wide'.

keyTakeaways: Attention lets every word decide which other words matter.
Models run many attention heads in parallel.

modules.title: The transformer block
modules.goal: See the whole machine: how tokens flow through a tall stack of identical blocks.
modules.summary: Embeddings pass through many identical blocks of attention and feed-forward layers, then become next-token probabilities. Bigger models add blocks and width.

simulation.name: Transformer builder
simulation.description: Set the number of blocks and the width; the simulation draws the stack, animates a token flowing through it and computes the parameter count and memory, next to real models (GPT-2 small, GPT-2 XL, GPT-3).
whatYouDo: Change blocks (1–96) and width (128–12,288)
Send a token through the stack
simulation.task: Rebuild GPT-2 small: 12 blocks, width 768 (about 124 million parameters).

keyTakeaways: Each block = attention (tokens talk to each other) + feed-forward (each token thinks alone).
Parameters grow with the number of blocks and with the width squared.

modules.title: Temperature and sampling
modules.goal: Learn how the model picks one word from its probabilities, and what temperature really does.
modules.summary: Temperature sharpens or flattens the probabilities; top-p removes the unlikely tail. The model's scores never change, only how we choose.

simulation.name: Sampling lab
simulation.description: Candidate next words for 'I like to drink a cup of …', from 'tea' to 'socks', shown as probability bars that react to temperature and top-p. Drawing 20 samples shows how often each word is picked.
whatYouDo: Move the temperature (0–2) and top-p sliders
Sample 20 words and compare
simulation.task: Sample at temperature 0, then at 1.5 or higher with top-p at 1.

keyTakeaways: Temperature 0 always takes the top word; higher means more variety and more risk.
This is why the same question can get different answers.

modules.title: Pre-training, fine-tuning and RLHF
modules.goal: Understand the three training stages that turn a text predictor into a helpful assistant.
modules.summary: Pre-training on trillions of words gives knowledge, fine-tuning teaches the assistant format, and preference tuning (RLHF) shapes answers to what people prefer.

simulation.name: Training stages and human rater
simulation.description: Three stage tabs show the training data, what the model learns and how it answers 'How do I boil an egg?' after each stage. In stage 3 you rate pairs of answers like the human raters behind RLHF.
whatYouDo: Compare the answer after each stage
Pick the better answer in three pairs
simulation.task: Visit all three stages and rate all three answer pairs.

keyTakeaways: A pre-trained base model only continues text.
Pre-training is by far the most expensive stage.

modules.title: KV cache and context length
modules.goal: Learn the trick that makes generating long answers fast, and why it eats so much memory.
modules.summary: Keys and values of earlier tokens never change, so they are cached. This saves huge amounts of work, but the cache grows with conversation length and the number of users.

simulation.name: KV cache stepper and memory calculator
simulation.description: Part 1 generates a sentence token by token, showing which keys and values are computed and which are reused, with a running count. Part 2 calculates the KV-cache memory for Llama 3 8B or 70B by conversation length and number of users.
whatYouDo: Generate tokens with and without the cache
Change the model, context length and users
simulation.task: Generate the full sentence without and with the cache (44 versus 9 computations).

keyTakeaways: With the cache, each new token costs about the same.
For long conversations the cache can need more memory than the model itself.

modules.title: Quantization: shrinking models
modules.goal: See how models are shrunk to fewer bits per weight, and the trick that keeps them accurate.
modules.summary: Weights are rounded to a few allowed values. Rare outliers stretch the scale and wreck accuracy; a separate scale per small group fixes it.

simulation.name: Quantization explorer
simulation.description: A histogram of 1,024 realistic weights (with optional outliers) before and after rounding, with the allowed values drawn in. Stats show the rounding error, the share of weights rounded to zero and the memory for a 70B model.
whatYouDo: Choose 8, 4, 3 or 2 bits
Switch between one scale per layer and one per group of 32
Toggle the outliers
simulation.task: With outliers, compare 4-bit per-layer and per-group scaling (the error drops about threefold).

keyTakeaways: Fewer bits = smaller and faster, but bigger rounding errors.
Per-group scales keep 4-bit models accurate.

labs.title: Neural Network Foundations
labs.description: Build and train small neural networks yourself: what a neuron is, how a network measures its mistakes, and how it learns by nudging its weights. Includes a free playground.

simulation.name: Neural network playground
simulation.description: A live network diagram where line colour and thickness show each weight and neuron colour shows its output. You can train step by step, watch an answer flow from input to output, inspect any neuron or connection with real numbers, tune weights by hand, and follow the mistake score on charts. A free playground offers six example models (doubling, Celsius to Fahrenheit, AND, XOR, absolute value, sine wave) with configurable hidden layers.
